processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Starting/general Fe–Mn–Al–C ingot preparation step preceding the Route-1 annealing-aging treatment.
Route 1 is applied to hot-rolled austenite-base Fe–Mn–Al–C steel.
The cooling rate after hot rolling strongly influences intergranular κ-carbide formation.
Isothermal annealing is the first treatment of Route 1 for austenite-base steels; figure_003 also shows a lower annealing interval of 600–800 °C.

Aging after annealing (Route 1) is beneficial to nano-precipitate nucleation; aging temperature and time should be precisely regulated to avoid intergranular κ*-carbide and β-Mn. figure_003 shows the aging stage at 450–700 °C.

structures.overall_structure: Room-temperature microstructure of the single austenite Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steel: equiaxed austenite together with annealing twins, because the thermal-mechanical processing temperature lies within the single austenite phase region; after aging, fine dispersed κ-carbide (intragranular κ0 and intergranular κ*) and B2/DO3 form.

precipitates.distribution: along the prior austenite grain boundary (intergranular)
formed in austenite depending on element contents and cooling rate

defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: The interaction between κ-carbides and dislocations does not change the plane-slip mode, but additional dislocation sources are activated and acted upon by cross slip; nano κ-carbides uniformly distribute in austenite and promote plane slip, and as strain increases the plane dislocation structure is further refined, contributing to continuous strain hardening.

interfaces.slip_behavior: Plane slip promoted by uniformly distributed nano κ-carbide; cross slip activates additional dislocation sources; the plane dislocation structure refines with increasing strain, giving continuous strain hardening.
interfaces.phase_evolution: On aging at 500–700 °C, spinodal decomposition occurs in austenite: γ → γ′ + γ″ → γ″ + L1₂ (short-range ordering phase) → γ′ + κ′.
interfaces.interface_notes: The κ-carbide/austenite interface is considered an effective hydrogen capture center; the presence of vacancies at this interface can improve hydrogen solubility. High aging temperature accelerates precipitation of coarse κ*-carbide along the grain boundary, and long aging time causes brittle β-Mn, both unfavorable to ductility/toughness.

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: Class-level: fine and dispersed carbides generate in single austenite-base Fe–Mn–Al–C steel (Al>7 wt% and C>0.7 wt%) after aging treatment, enhancing precipitation strengthening; κ-carbide significantly enhances yield strength without significantly deteriorating ductility but raises the yield ratio of Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels.

characterization_methods.purpose: Observe the distribution of κ-carbide along grain boundaries and within grains.
characterization_methods.key_findings: κ-carbide adopts intergranular (grain-boundary) and intragranular (within-grain) distributions in the austenite matrix, with bright grain-boundary networks decorated by κ particles.

characterization_methods.purpose: Identify κ-carbide along grain boundaries and within grains, its crystallographic relationship with the γ matrix, and γ_twin twins.
characterization_methods.key_findings: TEM/SAED confirms κ-carbide bands along boundaries (spots 100, 0ī1) and intragranular κ plates with γ_twin twins; κ adopts a hexagonal-ring spot pattern (spots 200, 101, 111, 110) around the transmitted spot.

analytical_models.equation_role: Predicts alloy density from Al, C and Mn mass fractions.
Relates austenite lattice constant to Al, C and Mn mass fractions.
Gives yield-strength increment of Fe–Mn–Al–C steel as a function of Al, Mn or C content (effects of C and Al stronger than Mn).

unmapped_findings: Constituent-phase windows defining the single austenite Fe–Mn–Al–C steel (Table 1): 15.0<X_Mn<30.0, 2.0<X_Al<12.0, 0.5<X_C<2.0 (wt.%), with constituent phases γ, α, δ, κ, β-Mn (b0041).

High C (>0.7 wt%) and Al (>7.0 wt%) contents are the primary conditions for κ-carbide formation in single austenite-base Fe–Mn–Al–C steels; κ-carbide formation is governed by the eutectoid reaction and its composition varies with aging conditions (b0071, b0070).

The deformation mechanism of single austenite-base Fe–Mn–Al–C steel is controlled by stacking-fault energy (SFE), shifting from TRIP to TWIP and then to MBIP/SIP with increasing Al content; figure_007 shows iso-SFE contours of 20 and 50 mJ/m² and a 'κ-carbide forming border' (b0082, b0088, figure_007).

Solid-solution strengthening of austenite: 1 wt% C contributes a yield-strength increment of 187–300 MPa, whereas 1 wt% Al contributes slightly below 10 MPa (b0061); this is class-level rather than a property of a single annealed-aged specimen.

Specific single-austenite example alloys cited in the review (each a distinct alloy, not the generic annealed-aged sample): Fe-30Mn-11Al-1.2C shows 1058 MPa yield strength, 1310 MPa tensile strength and 38% total elongation [137] (b0140); Park et al. [87] quenched Fe-28Mn-Al-(0.8–1.0)C (MBIP) reached 873 MPa tensile strength and 100% total elongation (b0091); Welsch et al. [88] Fe-30.4Mn-8Al-1.2C (SFE 85 mJ/m², DSBR) reached 900 MPa tensile strength and 68% total elongation (b0091).

Both fine intragranular and intergranular κ-carbide significantly enhance the yield strength without significantly deteriorating ductility but increase the yield ratio (>0.8) of Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels (b0140).
Long aging time leads to formation of brittle β-Mn phase, and intergranular κ*-carbide and β-Mn are unfavorable to the ductility and toughness of Fe–Mn–Al–C low-density steels (b0071).

Cryogenic/interfacial note: hydrogen embrittlement in κ-carbide-bearing austenitic steel depends on C and Mn contents of κ-carbide; increasing C and reducing Mn in κ-carbide is recommended to control hydrogen diffusion (b0130).
